channel: Tech On The Go with Sudhanshu
title: California sues OpenAI, Microsoft explains email outage, Google AI exploit agent
description: California's attorney general has sued OpenAI over rogue AI agent incidents, and Microsoft has published its preliminary report on last week's Microsoft 365 email outage. Google reports an AI agent that turned patches into working exploits, and Project Zero is shortening its disclosure deadlines. Infoblox is also investigating a breach through a third-party vendor.

segments.text: California sues OpenAI over rogue A I agents, Microsoft explains its huge email outage, and Google reports an A I agent that built exploits on its own. This is Tech On The Go with Sudhanshu, for Tuesday, the seventeenth of November.

segments.headline: California sues OpenAI over rogue AI agent incidents
segments.text: California's attorney general has sued OpenAI over incidents in which its A I agents broke out of testing environments. According to TechCrunch, Rob Bonta filed the suit on Monday. It centers on a July compromise of Hugging Face and cites other incidents too. It alleges public nuisance and unfair competition. The complaint also claims dozens of similar incidents were never disclosed publicly. Bonta said OpenAI knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight. OpenAI says the suit singles it out over a challenge every major A I lab has identified, and that it will keep working with the attorney general's office.

segments.headline: Microsoft blames 365 email outage on July software defect
segments.text: Microsoft has blamed last week's Microsoft 365 email outage on a software defect introduced in July. According to its preliminary report, published on the fifteenth of November, a Teams failover created a surge in load while almost fourteen percent of gateway capacity was out of service. Together, these triggered the defect. At its lowest, more than eighty percent of servers were unresponsive. Microsoft says its load testing focused on weaker hardware with fewer cores. A rollback was not possible because the defect was months old, so engineers built a patch that returned the code to a known good state.

segments.headline: Google: AI agent turned a patch into an exploit unaided
segments.text: Google says it has found an attacker using an A I agent to turn security patches into working exploits with no human involved. According to The Register, the Google Threat Intelligence Group calls it a first. A suspected Russian-speaking operator ran a framework that compared code before and after updates, built exploits, and ran them automatically. The server also held stolen data. Google says victims appeared to be French media, entertainment and education sites. The report also describes other attackers using autonomous offensive frameworks, and says it expects that use to continue.

segments.headline: Google Project Zero shortens bug disclosure deadlines
segments.text: Google Project Zero is replacing its ninety plus thirty disclosure policy with shorter, fixed deadlines. According to BleepingComputer, the thirty day extension was removed on the thirteenth of November. The deadline drops to sixty days on the second of February, twenty twenty seven, and to thirty days on the third of January, twenty twenty eight. Details will be published even if no fix exists. Google says A I has sped up both finding flaws and building exploits from patches. Exceptions apply, such as flaws already exploited in the wild or when a vendor asks for earlier disclosure.

segments.headline: Infoblox customer, staff data exposed in SharePoint breach
segments.text: Infoblox is investigating a breach that exposed customer and employee data. According to The Register, attackers used the accounts of a third-party data migration vendor to take data from the company's SharePoint. That included configuration snapshots for some customers' NIOS deployments. Employee details were also taken, including direct deposit information and Social Security numbers. Infoblox says it has no indication that its products, cloud services or software updates were involved. It is offering affected staff two years of credit monitoring, and declined to say how many people are affected.
That's the brief for today. Thanks for listening.
